items.prompt: A workload tolerates eight hours of downtime and four hours of data loss. Which recovery pattern is a reasonable starting point?
constraints: Data can be restored from backups.
The restore process can be tested.

options.text: Backup and restore with measured backup age, restore duration, dependency setup, and validation.
Active-active Regions with synchronous user traffic everywhere.
No recovery copy because the RTO is relaxed.
Warm standby with full production capacity regardless of objectives.

feedback.Reason: Relaxed objectives can fit a cold restore strategy when measured recovery meets them.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Backup-and-restore keeps recoverable data but provisions and restores the serving environment during an incident.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team tests backup age, restore time, quotas, validation, and traffic return against the eight-hour and four-hour limits.
Details.errorCorrection: A relaxed RTO does not remove data protection, and more expensive tiers are not required without a tighter objective.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Restore duration grows with data and dependency size, so the pattern needs repeated evidence.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Active-active is not justified by relaxed objectives and adds complexity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Without a copy, data cannot be recovered.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Full warm capacity may be unnecessary cost for this requirement.

items.prompt: A recovery Region keeps replicated databases and core configuration ready but launches application capacity during a disaster. Which pattern is this?
constraints: The application fleet is not serving normal traffic.
Data and core services remain available.

options.text: Pilot light: keep a minimal running core and expand the application during recovery.
Active-active: both Regions serve production continuously.
Backup-and-restore: no data or infrastructure is prepared.
Warm standby: a scaled production environment serves continuously.

feedback.Reason: Pilot light keeps the essential data or core components ready while application capacity is created during recovery.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The standby minimizes running cost but requires automated provisioning and validation before traffic can move.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team maintains replicated data, launches the application tier, tests dependencies, and measures scale-out time against RTO.
Details.errorCorrection: Active-active serves concurrently, backup-and-restore starts from copies, and warm standby keeps more serving capacity ready.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Pilot light has lower cost than warm standby but longer recovery and more bootstrap risk.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Concurrent production service is active-active, not pilot light.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Prepared core resources distinguish pilot light from a cold restore.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Warm standby has a scaled ready environment rather than only a core.

items.prompt: A secondary Region runs a reduced but functional application fleet, receives replicated data, and can scale to production load after a controlled traffic shift. Which pattern fits?

options.text: Warm standby, with tested scale-out, data replication, health validation, and traffic cutover.
Cold backup, because no traffic is served in the secondary.
Pilot light, because every warm standby must have zero application capacity.
Active-active, because any replicated data means both Regions are equal.

feedback.Reason: Warm standby keeps a reduced serving environment ready and expands it during a failure.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The standby has running application capacity, unlike pilot light, but may not match primary scale until recovery actions complete.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner tests scale-up, dependency readiness, data lag, and routing before claiming the RTO.
Details.errorCorrection: No serving environment is cold backup, pilot light has a smaller core, and replication alone does not make active-active.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Warm standby reduces RTO versus pilot light at higher steady cost.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Running a reduced application is more than a cold backup.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Pilot light does not require the reduced serving fleet described.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Active-active requires concurrent production serving and coordinated data behavior.

items.prompt: A global application must continue serving during a Region failure with minimal traffic interruption. Both Regions serve production and data conflicts are controlled. Which pattern is appropriate?
constraints: Data ownership or conflict resolution is designed.
Traffic can be shifted or distributed.

options.text: Active-active, with health-based routing, capacity in both Regions, and a tested data consistency and conflict strategy.
Backup-and-restore, because a backup is sufficient for zero interruption.
Pilot light, because only replicated data is needed during normal operation.
A single-AZ deployment with more instances.

feedback.Reason: Active-active uses both Regions for production and can reduce failover interruption when data and routing semantics are correct.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Concurrent serving requires capacity, health routing, data replication or partitioning, and conflict handling in both locations.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team tests regional withdrawal, traffic distribution, writes, reconciliation, and capacity under the remaining Region's load.
Details.errorCorrection: Backups and pilot light require recovery actions, and more instances in one AZ do not cover a Region failure.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Active-active has the highest operational and data-consistency complexity and cost.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A backup requires restore time and cannot guarantee zero interruption.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Pilot light does not normally serve production traffic from both Regions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: One AZ remains a failure-domain dependency.

items.prompt: A workload needs a 15-minute RTO, but the current design restores from a large backup in two hours. Which change is most direct?
constraints: Data can be replicated to another Region.
Cost can increase for this tier.

options.text: Move toward pilot light or warm standby with pre-positioned data, automated infrastructure, and tested cutover instead of relying on a cold restore.
Keep backup-and-restore and shorten the RTO in the documentation.
Increase DNS TTL to speed up propagation.
Add more backup retention without improving restore readiness.

feedback.Reason: A two-hour cold restore cannot meet a 15-minute RTO without changing recovery readiness and automation.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Pre-positioned data and infrastructure reduce restore and bootstrap time, leaving validation and traffic transition within the objective.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect selects a recovery tier, provisions quotas and dependencies, and repeatedly measures the end-to-end cutover.
Details.errorCorrection: Documentation cannot change elapsed time, DNS TTL does not restore services, and more retention does not reduce restore duration.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Ready capacity and replication add cost and require stronger operational controls.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Renaming the target does not shorten restore time.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: TTL affects caching, not data and application recovery.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Retention protects history but does not make recovery faster.

items.prompt: A backup job completes successfully but its age at the time of the last test exceeded the business RPO. What is the correct conclusion?
constraints: The business RPO is stricter than the observed backup age.

options.text: The design passes because the backup job has a successful status.
The design fails the RPO; increase protection frequency or use replication and retest the recoverable point.
The design passes if the backup is encrypted.
Change the RPO to match the backup schedule without business approval.

feedback.Reason: A successful backup job does not prove that the recoverable point is recent enough.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: RPO is evaluated from data freshness at recovery, not from the job's completion status alone.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner measures backup age and restore output under realistic timing and changes the mechanism when the gap exceeds the requirement.
Details.errorCorrection: Encryption and job success do not imply freshness, and changing a business requirement requires approval.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More frequent backups or replication add cost and may affect throughput.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.A: Successful completion does not establish an acceptable recovery point.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: The target cannot be changed silently to fit implementation.

items.prompt: A warm standby is ready, but the team has no tested method to move users from the failed Region. What is missing?
constraints: DNS or global routing can direct traffic.

options.text: A tested health and traffic transition procedure with TTL, routing policy, validation, rollback, and operator ownership.
Only a lower DNS TTL set during the incident.
A second backup copy with no routing change.
A statement that clients will discover the standby automatically.

feedback.Reason: Ready compute is not serving capacity until traffic can be moved safely and verified.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Cutover includes routing, health, DNS caching, application validation, and a reversal path.
Details.scenarioApplication: The runbook shifts traffic in a controlled way, checks user SLIs, and records when rollback is required.
Details.errorCorrection: TTL alone does not perform a cutover, backups do not route traffic, and clients do not discover arbitrary endpoints.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: DNS changes have cache delay, so a lower TTL before the incident and an alternate routing mechanism may be needed.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: TTL controls cache duration but is not a complete transition procedure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A copy does not move user traffic.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Clients need an explicit endpoint and routing mechanism.

items.prompt: Two active Regions accept updates to the same customer record and later produce conflicting values. What must the design add?

options.text: Define write ownership, conflict resolution, ordering or idempotency, and reconciliation before claiming active-active correctness.
Assume last writer wins is always acceptable without business review.
Stop replicating data while keeping both Regions writable.
Use a shorter DNS TTL to resolve record conflicts.

feedback.Reason: Concurrent serving does not solve multi-writer consistency; data semantics must define what happens when writes conflict.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Active-active needs partitioning, single-writer ownership, conflict-free operations, or a business-approved reconciliation rule.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team tests concurrent updates, retries, replay, and regional isolation and makes conflict outcomes observable.
Details.errorCorrection: Last-writer-wins can lose meaningful updates, stopping replication breaks convergence, and DNS does not resolve data conflicts.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Strong coordination can increase latency or reduce independence, while conflict resolution adds application complexity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Conflict policy must match business correctness and cannot be assumed.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Writable isolated copies diverge without a convergence strategy.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Routing cache duration does not define data merge semantics.

items.prompt: A ransomware scenario requires recovery from an earlier clean point even if production credentials are compromised. Which backup control helps?
constraints: The recovery copy must survive production deletion.
The restore point must be selected and verified.

options.text: Use logically or account-isolated backups with protected retention and separate recovery permissions, then test restore and clean-point selection.
Keep backups in the same writable account with the same administrator credentials.
Disable backup deletion protection to make recovery faster.
Use only the newest backup regardless of compromise evidence.

feedback.Reason: Recovery copies must be protected from the failure or compromise that affects production and must be usable at a known clean point.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Cross-account or logically air-gapped controls, retention, and least-privilege restore access reduce correlated deletion risk.
Details.scenarioApplication: Operators identify a clean recovery point, restore into an isolated environment, validate integrity, and only then return service.
Details.errorCorrection: Shared credentials allow correlated compromise, disabling protection increases deletion risk, and newest is not always clean.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Isolation adds administration and recovery coordination but protects the recovery boundary.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Shared administration creates correlated compromise risk.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Removing deletion protection weakens recovery safety.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Recency alone does not establish integrity or cleanliness.

items.prompt: A pilot-light recovery takes too long because operators manually create the application tier and security rules. What is the best improvement?
constraints: The core data is already replicated.
Manual steps are the RTO bottleneck.

options.text: Automate infrastructure and configuration creation from versioned definitions, then validate the bootstrap path in recovery exercises.
Add more people to perform the same manual steps during an incident.
Remove security rules from the recovery environment.
Change the pilot light label to warm standby.

feedback.Reason: Automation reduces repeatable bootstrap time and variation in a pilot-light recovery path.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Infrastructure as code and versioned configuration make recovery steps repeatable and testable before an incident.
Details.scenarioApplication: The pipeline creates the application tier, permissions, routes, and scaling settings and measures completion and validation.
Details.errorCorrection: More operators do not remove manual coordination, removing security is unsafe, and naming does not change readiness.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Automation itself needs testing, artifact availability, and permissions in the recovery Region.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: More manual labor can still be slow and inconsistent.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Security controls are part of a usable recovery environment.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A label change does not provision capacity.

items.prompt: A warm standby has enough capacity for normal background traffic but not for the full primary load. What must the recovery design include?

options.text: Pre-validate scale limits, quotas, launch time, health checks, and capacity headroom, then test scale-out under recovery traffic.
Assume the standby is full capacity because it is already running.
Disable autoscaling to prevent changes during failover.
Send all traffic immediately before scaling begins.

feedback.Reason: Warm standby readiness includes the ability to expand safely and quickly to the load it will receive.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Recovery capacity depends on scaling limits, launch time, service quotas, health, and traffic transition as well as running instances.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team exercises a primary failure, scales the standby, validates user SLIs, and adjusts headroom or the RTO from evidence.
Details.errorCorrection: Partial capacity is not full capacity, disabling scaling removes recovery flexibility, and unprepared traffic can overload the standby.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More pre-running capacity reduces scale-out risk but increases cost.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Running a reduced fleet does not prove full-load capacity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Autoscaling may be required to meet recovered demand.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Traffic should follow validated capacity, not precede it blindly.

items.prompt: An active-active design loses one Region. Which capacity assumption must be validated?
constraints: The remaining Region must serve critical traffic.
The failed Region's traffic is rerouted.

options.text: The remaining Region must have tested capacity, quotas, dependencies, and data behavior for the redirected load, not only its normal share.
Only DNS health is needed because active-active has no capacity concern.
The remaining Region can exceed every quota during recovery.
Reduce monitoring so more capacity is available.

feedback.Reason: Active-active reduces recovery time only if one surviving Region can absorb the failure scenario.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Regional failover changes traffic share, resource utilization, quotas, and dependency load in the survivor.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team tests withdrawal of one Region, observes saturation and data correctness, and retains headroom or load-sheds lower-priority work.
Details.errorCorrection: DNS does not create capacity, quotas cannot be exceeded by intent, and hiding metrics removes evidence.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Overprovisioning for a full regional failure raises cost but is necessary for the claimed availability tier.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Routing health cannot substitute for survivor capacity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Service limits still apply during recovery.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Monitoring does not create meaningful capacity and is needed for safe recovery.

items.prompt: Cross-Region backups are present, but the recovery Region cannot decrypt them because the required KMS key is unavailable. What should the plan include?
constraints: The target Region must restore them.
Key access is a recovery dependency.

options.text: Pre-provision or replicate the required key and permissions in the target, document key dependencies, and test encrypted restore there.
Assume the primary Region's KMS key is automatically usable everywhere.
Disable encryption on production backups.
Copy only the backup metadata and restore without the key.

feedback.Reason: Encryption keys and their authorization are part of the recoverable system and must exist in the recovery path.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Regional KMS keys and policies are dependencies for decrypting encrypted recovery copies.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team provisions target keys or supported replicas, grants recovery roles, and performs a real encrypted restore before claiming readiness.
Details.errorCorrection: Keys are not automatically global, disabling encryption weakens protection, and metadata cannot decrypt ciphertext.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Key replication and administration require governance, separation of duties, and careful access control.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: KMS key scope and policy must be handled in the target Region.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Removing encryption trades a recovery dependency for a security failure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Encrypted data requires the appropriate key material and permission.

items.prompt: A warm standby has a one-minute replication lag, while the business RPO is five minutes. What does this evidence show?
constraints: The lag is measured during representative load.
Restore and traffic cutover are separately tested.

options.text: The observed data lag is within the RPO, but the full design still needs restore, application, routing, and failure testing.
The entire RTO is proven because data lag is low.
The design is active-active because replication is under five minutes.
No further testing is needed.

feedback.Reason: Replication lag is evidence for RPO, not proof of the whole recovery objective or architecture.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: RPO concerns recoverable data freshness; RTO also includes service readiness, validation, and traffic transition.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team records lag under load and separately measures recovery duration and user behavior after a failure.
Details.errorCorrection: Low lag does not prove RTO, active-active requires serving behavior, and readiness claims need tests.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Replication can consume bandwidth and affect source performance, so measurements should include peak and failure conditions.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: RTO includes more than data replication lag.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Replication cadence does not define concurrent serving.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Untested dependencies and cutover remain unknown.

items.prompt: A cutover to a warm standby succeeds, but data validation finds an application bug in the recovered version. What should the runbook provide?
constraints: The prior primary is isolated but intact.

options.text: A controlled rollback or forward-fix decision with traffic fencing, data reconciliation, and an owner-approved safety procedure.
Immediately switch traffic back without stopping writes in the standby.
Delete the standby so operators cannot choose it again.
Ignore validation because traffic is already flowing.

feedback.Reason: Recovery cutover can expose application or data defects and needs a safe reversal or forward-fix path.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Traffic fencing and write ownership prevent split-brain while operators decide how to reconcile data and route users.
Details.scenarioApplication: The runbook pauses or isolates writes, selects rollback or forward fix, validates data, and records the transition.
Details.errorCorrection: Uncoordinated reverse traffic can create divergence, deletion removes options, and passing traffic is not proof of correctness.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Rollback may be harder after new writes, so data ownership and cutover checkpoints must be explicit.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Concurrent writes can create split-brain and reconciliation risk.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Deletion destroys recovery capacity and evidence.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Traffic flow does not prove data correctness.

items.prompt: Which consideration most directly distinguishes warm standby from active-active for a workload with a short but nonzero RTO?
constraints: The standby may serve limited traffic.
The business accepts a controlled cutover.

options.text: Warm standby can cost less because the secondary runs reduced capacity and is activated or scaled during recovery; active-active serves both Regions continuously.
Warm standby always has zero RTO and active-active always loses data.
The two patterns are identical if both have backups.
Active-active requires no data or routing design.

feedback.Reason: The distinction is concurrent production serving and readiness level, which affects cost, cutover, and data complexity.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Warm standby keeps reduced ready capacity, while active-active keeps both locations serving and requires concurrent traffic and data semantics.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect chooses warm standby when controlled cutover and some scale-out fit the RTO and budget.
Details.errorCorrection: Neither pattern guarantees a fixed outcome without tests, and backups do not define the pattern.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Active-active can reduce interruption but increases cost, consistency, and operational complexity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Both patterns need evidence and can be designed with different data objectives.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Backup presence does not make recovery tiers identical.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Active-active requires explicit routing and data behavior.

items.prompt: A recovery Region receives traffic after DNS failover, but only the home page is checked. What additional validation is needed?
constraints: The recovery is intended for real users.

options.text: Run representative read and write journeys, validate dependencies and data integrity, and monitor customer SLIs after the switch.
Check only that the DNS record changed.
Assume successful TCP connections prove the application is recovered.
Disable writes permanently in the recovery Region.

feedback.Reason: Traffic routing and a shallow endpoint do not prove that the recovered user journey is correct.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Recovery validation must exercise authentication, dependencies, reads, writes, correctness, and user-facing latency.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team uses safe test data and production-like checks, then watches SLIs and reconciliation during the first recovery period.
Details.errorCorrection: DNS and TCP prove only lower layers, and disabling writes changes product behavior rather than validating it.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Representative tests need protected credentials and safe data cleanup.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A DNS change does not prove serving correctness.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: TCP reachability does not test application behavior.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Permanent write disablement is not a general recovery solution.

items.prompt: A workload has grown from a small internal service to a customer-critical platform. What should happen to its recovery pattern?
constraints: The original backup strategy remains unchanged.
The new requirement must be evidence-based.

options.text: Reassess RTO, RPO, traffic, dependencies, cost, and tested recovery results; then move to a more ready pattern if the evidence requires it.
Keep backup-and-restore permanently because the pattern was once approved.
Copy the same backup to more buckets without measuring restore time.
Declare active-active without changing serving or data behavior.

feedback.Reason: Recovery architecture should evolve when business impact and objectives change.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Pattern selection is a trade-off among RTO, RPO, readiness, cost, data semantics, and operational evidence.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner reviews current demand and exercises the existing path before selecting pilot light, warm standby, or active-active improvements.
Details.errorCorrection: Approval becomes stale, more copies do not prove fast restore, and a label does not create concurrent serving.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Higher readiness adds cost and complexity and should be justified by the criticality increase.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A changed business tier invalidates an unchanged recovery assumption.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Copy count does not prove restore duration or usability.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Active-active is an operational and data design, not a declaration.
